title: Add keras_model_to_estimator()
description:
Allows conversion of Keras models to TF estimators.

TODO after merge:
1. Figure out how this would work with `export_savedmodel()`, hopefully it'll be as simple as obtaining the input tensor (see https://github.com/rstudio/tfestimators/pull/132)
2. Add docs. Thinking of an article under *Advanced* at https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/tfestimators/articles/simplify_function.html

Example usage with `tfdatasets`:
```
library(keras)
use_implementation("tensorflow")
library(tfdatasets)
library(tfestimators)

# define and compile keras model
model <- keras_model_sequential() %>%
  layer_dense(units = 256, activation = 'relu', input_shape = c(784)) %>%
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 128, activation = 'relu') %>%
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.3) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 10, activation = 'softmax')

model %>% compile(
  loss = 'categorical_crossentropy',
  optimizer = optimizer_rmsprop(),
  metrics = c('accuracy')
)

# obtain input and output names from keras model
input_name <- model$input_names
output_name <- model$output_names

# function to read and preprocess mnist dataset
mnist_dataset <- function(filename, shuffle = TRUE, epochs = NULL, batch_size = 128) {
  dataset <- tfrecord_dataset(filename) %>%
    dataset_map(function(example_proto) {
      
      # parse record
      features <- tf$parse_single_example(
        example_proto,
        features = list(
          image_raw = tf$FixedLenFeature(shape(), tf$string),
          label = tf$FixedLenFeature(shape(), tf$int64)
        )
      )
      
      # preprocess image
      image <- tf$decode_raw(features$image_raw, tf$uint8)
      image <- tf$cast(image, tf$float32) / 255
      image$set_shape(shape(784))
      
      # convert label to one-hot
      label <- tf$one_hot(tf$cast(features$label, tf$int32), 10L) %>%
        tf$cast(tf$float32)
      
      # return
      setNames(list(image, label), c(input_name, output_name))
    }) %>%
    dataset_repeat(epochs)
  
  if (shuffle) dataset <- dataset_shuffle(dataset, 10000)
  
  dataset %>%
    dataset_batch(batch_size)
}

model %>% compile(
  loss = 'categorical_crossentropy',
  optimizer = optimizer_rmsprop(),
  metrics = c('accuracy')
)

model_est <- keras_model_to_estimator(model)

history <- model_est %>%
  train(input_fn(mnist_dataset("mnist/train.tfrecords"), 
                 features = input_name,
                 response = output_name), steps = 100L)

evaluation_result <- model_est %>%
  evaluate(input_fn(mnist_dataset("mnist/validation.tfrecords",
                                  shuffle = FALSE,
                                  epochs = 1),
                    features = input_name,
                    response = output_name))

```

title: Make export_savedmodel() use raw tensors
description:
Back when `export_savedmodel()` was implemented in `tfestimators`, the [build_parsing_serving_input_receiver_fn](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/estimator/export/build_parsing_serving_input_receiver_fn) was used, while not incorrect, this input function expects a [tf.Example](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/r1.4/tensorflow/core/example/example.proto) which happens to be a protobuf structure that can be constructed using a few helpers like `tf.parse_example()`; however, passing protobuf structures is not straightforward to use nor compatible with other `export_savedmodel()` implementations.

Instead, this PR switches the implementation to use [build_raw_serving_input_receiver_fn](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/estimator/export/build_raw_serving_input_receiver_fn) which requires raw tensors that are compatible with other package implementations. A good example that informs this implementaiton was found under [/tensorflow/models/official/mnist/](https://github.com/tensorflow/models/blob/72f5834cc19bcfd3aef795dd926575fd9e0db802/official/mnist/mnist.py).
  
However, since multiple input/output tensors support was added until TF 1.4 (see [/tensorflow/issues/12367](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/issues/12367#issuecomment-335320352)), this change fallbacks to parsing serving input as protobuf inputs for earlier versions.

title: inform user when coercing factor levels to [0, n] range
Initial work on `train_and_evaluate()`
description:
This PR adds support for `train_and_evaluate()` for estimators. Though they are not exported yet until they are more stable. 

A couple of questions:

1. For `train_spec` and `eval_spec`, we'd want to integrate with `tfruns` by adding the view_metrics, history, etc. into the hooks. We can use [these methods](https://github.com/rstudio/tfestimators/blob/master/R/utils_tf.R#L112-L141) that I refactored earlier from `train()` and `evaluate()` that can be re-used by `train_spec` and `eval_spec`. However, I want to double check with you to see if you have any concerns that `.globals$history` that we are using to save training history and metrics may not work correctly under distributed settings. 

2. Do you have concerns over the fact that `train_spec` and `eval_spec` are lazily evaluated (on the R side only) since we need to toggle the correct input_fn to use using the `estimator`'s class inside `train_and_evaluate()`. 

3. The default for `train_spec`'s `max_steps` is `NULL` in Python API,  which trains forever (same behavior as `train.tf_estimator`). Do you think we should change this to something small (e.g. `2`) on the R side? This will perhaps make it less confusing for R users but on the other hand inconsistent with the Python API. What are your opinions?

A couple of TODOs:

1. A vignette for example usages for local and distributed settings. 
2. Support additional arguments for `verbose` and `view_metrics` to integrate with tfruns.

title: Add simplify function for predict() and evaluate()
description:
This addresses https://github.com/rstudio/tfestimators/issues/49. @jjallaire This is a little bit different than the original approach you outlined:

*  "We provide a hook for custom estimators to provide a simplifier (perhaps this is attached to model_fn, perhaps via an S3 method)" - instead of doing this, here we are taking directly from the predictions result and apply a function to them. I think this is the easier to maintain and easiest for users to follow to write their own functions. 

* Users should be able to provide their own function for simplification. For package maintainer or canned estimator implementors, they can write a method like `predict.tf_estimator_dnn_linear_combined_classifier()` to override the existing `predict.tf_estimator()` since a canned estimator has multiple classes (I need to experiment to see what the order/priority of execution would be for an object with multiple classes in order to do this correctly):
```
> class(clf)
[1] "tf_estimator"                                "tf_estimator_classifier"                    
[3] "tf_estimator_dnn_linear_combined_classifier"
```
This allows the implementation of `predict()` to be model type level (multihead, time series, clustering) instead of per canned estimator level. I am uncertain whether this is the right approach so I opened this PR for comments and suggestions. 

* Should the default of `simplify` be `FALSE` for backward compatibility purposes? From another perspective, set default to be `TRUE` lowers the entry of barrier for a lot of users, especially new users.

title: Add support to save models through `tf_save()`
description:
Adds support for `tf_save(model, path)`, currently, implemented in `tfestimators` but once the model is proven in `keras`, we would move this signature to `tensorflow`.

The idea behind `tf_save()` is to allow users to export models with ease. This requires each package to provide a `tf_save_spec_from_model()` which will provide a default conversion from a model to a save specification. In most cases, the default specification is enough for proper interoperability. In other cases, explicit specifications would have to be created using `tf_save_regressor_spec()` and `tf_save_classification_spec()`.

A simple example to train and save a model, which could be reused in TensorFlow Serving, follows:

```r
library(tfestimators)
model <- linear_regressor(
 feature_columns = feature_columns( 
    column_numeric("disp", "cyl")
  )
)

mtcars_input_fn <- function(data) {
  input_fn(data, 
           features = c("disp", "cyl"), 
           response = "mpg")
}

model %>% train(mtcars_input_fn(train), steps = 1)
  
tf_save(model, tempdir())
```

title: Integration with tfruns package
description:
Changes to integrate with the active `run_dir()` from tfruns:

We no longer explicitly call the `run_dir()` function to determine the run_dir. Rather, if the user has left `model_dir = NULL` *and* a run_dir is in use (either because the user has called `use_run_dir()` explicitly or because a training supervisor like CloudML or GuildAI has set the `TENSORFLOW_RUN_DIR` environment variable) then it is used.

The idea here is that code which has no knowledge of run directories can actually benefit from them without explicitly opting in.

We also add a `model_dir()` function which can probe an estimator for it's model_dir (e.g. to pass to tensorboard or to use in `export_savedmodel()`).

Note that this implementation assumes that an R script will generally create a single model. If we want to support multiple models we could either:

1. Encourage users with multiple models to provision the run_dir appropriately, e.g.

    model_1_dir <- file.path(run_dir(), "model_1")
    model_2_dir <- file.path(run_dir(), "model_2")

2. *Always* create a subdirectory within the run_dir() for a new model.

I can see `print.tf_custom_model()` is necessary because it's useful to know what configs are used and whether a model is trained but I am not sure about `print. tf_custom_model_evaluation()` or `print.tf_custom_model_prediction()`.
